code: # exogenous probabilities p_math <- .1 # probability of passing math exam p_history <- .9 # probability of passing history  # structural equation causal_rule <- 'history & math' # Alice passes if she passes history and math  # collect the above information in a causal model causalmodel <- list(graduate=causal_rule, math=p_math, history=p_history)  # what happened in the actual world actual_world <- list(graduate=1, math=1, history=1) # to what extent did passing the history exam (high-probability event) cause  # Alice to graduate? compute_judgment(   'history', 'graduate', causalmodel, actual_world, 'ces', .7   ) #> [1] 0.2739082  # to what extent did passing the math exam (low-probability event) cause  # Alice to graduate? compute_judgment(   'math', 'graduate', causalmodel, actual_world, 'ces', .7   ) #> [1] 0.9472197

title: Computational models of causal judgment
text: Computing causal judgment requires three steps: -Specify causal model, -Specify happened actual world, -Request causal judgment. example, suppose Alice graduate passes History Math exam. Math exam difficult History exam easy. specify information causal model: string 'history & math' specifies structural equation graduate variable. variables history math associated prior probability. Next specify happens actual world; Alice passed History Math, graduates: Finally request causal judgment: first two arguments say want see extent math caused graduate. next two arguments specify causal model actual-world value variables (defined ). fifth argument specifies computational model want use (, CES). last argument specifies value stability parameter ss (much counterfactual simulation ‘anchored’ actual world). argument optional, default s=0s=0. Running command return ‘causal score’ -1 1 (CES) 0 1 (NS). Higher values indicate higher actual causal strength. CES model, negative value like -.8 indicates weak causal score, something like ‘negative’ causation. -.8 weaker example -.4. examples provided vignette. References: Icard, Kominsky & Knobe (2017). Normality actual causal strength. Cognition. Quillien & Lucas (2023). Counterfactuals logic causal selection. Psychological Review.
code: p_math <- .1 # probability of passing math exam p_history <- .9 # probability of passing history causal_rule <- 'history & math' # Alice passes if she passes history and math # collect the above information in a causal model causalmodel <- list(graduate=causal_rule, math=p_math, history=p_history) actual_world <- list(graduate=1, math=1, history=1) # to what extent did passing the math exam cause Alice to graduate? compute_judgment('math', 'graduate', causalmodel, actual_world, 'ces', .7)
